PromptPAR on ITCPR: Out-of-Distribution Collapse Analysis

Evaluating zero-shot pedestrian attribute recognition on a real-world surveillance dataset

📅 2026-06-04 🗂 ITCPR Gallery — 20,510 images 🔵 Checkpoint: PA100k (26 attrs) 🟣 Checkpoint: PETA (35 attrs) 📏 Sources: Celeb-reID · PRCC · LAST

📋 Executive Summary

PromptPAR collapses severely on ITCPR. The PA100k checkpoint produces only 7 distinct prediction sets for 20,508 images — 84% of all images receive exactly the same attribute list. The PETA checkpoint is less extreme (647 sets) but still highly degenerate. Both checkpoints show pairwise cosine similarity >0.94 between random image pairs.

ITCPR is a real-world surveillance dataset (Celeb-reID + PRCC + LAST) that is strongly out-of-distribution relative to the PA100k and PETA training sets. The images are low-resolution surveillance crops (typically 128×256 px) being fed to a model trained on clean, controlled pedestrian photographs. The result is a model that ignores image content and outputs a fixed set of majority-class attributes for every person.

The two checkpoints exhibit different failure modes: PA100k is catastrophically collapsed (7 output clusters, gender completely dead), while PETA is moderately collapsed (clothing attributes saturated, but age/gender/shoes show partial discrimination).

📉 Per-Image Variance

PA100k per-image std spans only 0.27–0.34 with mean 0.31. This extremely narrow range confirms the model is largely ignoring image content. PETA is slightly better (0.31–0.41, mean 0.36) but still severely constrained.

📂 Per-Source Breakdown

All three sources (Celeb-reID, PRCC, LAST) show nearly identical collapse patterns, ruling out camera-specific artifacts as the sole cause. PRCC shows slightly less collapse — its images are somewhat higher quality and more controlled than the other two sources.

🔍 Root Cause Analysis

1. Resolution and Visual Quality Mismatch (Primary)

ITCPR images are 128×256 px or smaller surveillance crops, upsampled to 224×224 for inference. This produces blurry, pixelated inputs with low contrast. PA100k and PETA training images are clear, well-lit pedestrian photographs. The CLIP visual encoder + visual prompts (trained end-to-end on clean images) have never seen this kind of degraded input — all surveillance images map to a narrow cluster in feature space.

2. Camera Angle and Viewpoint Prior

PA100k and PETA are dominated by front-facing pedestrian images, with a minority of side/back views. ITCPR is real surveillance footage where cameras often capture people from the side or back. The result: back fires for 99.8% of PA100k predictions, indicating the model interprets any non-frontal image as "back." The training set prior — not the image content — drives this.

3. Training-Set Distribution Leakage

backpack fires for 95% of PA100k images despite being a contextually uncommon attribute in a surveillance gallery. This reveals that the PA100k training set contained a high proportion of backpack-wearing subjects, and the model learned a prior rather than a detector. Similarly, PETA's upper casual + upper other are the "catch-all" categories that cover nearly every image in the training set.

4. Visual Prompt Over-Fitting

PromptPAR uses 50 visual prompts and 3 text prompts jointly fine-tuned on the training dataset. These prompts encode dataset-specific statistics rather than domain-invariant features. When applied to OOD surveillance images, they steer the attention mechanism toward the same spurious features regardless of image content.

5. Attribute Vocabulary Mismatch

PA100k/PETA vocabularies were designed for controlled pedestrian recognition. Attributes like upper splice, lower stripe, and long coat are well-represented in training data but may not apply to the clothing styles captured in ITCPR's surveillance footage. The model's text heads for rare attributes never learned to fire on OOD visual features.

Why is PETA better than PA100k on ITCPR? PETA has a larger attribute vocabulary (35 vs 26) including gender (male) and more granular age attributes. Its text prompts were trained to distinguish more fine-grained categories, giving the model more "slots" to assign probability mass. Even under collapse, the PETA vocabulary captures more meaningful variation (shoes, accessories, age).

✅ Conclusion & Recommendations

Neither checkpoint is usable zero-shot on ITCPR. PA100k is catastrophically collapsed (7 prediction clusters, gender dead). PETA is less extreme but still unusable for real discrimination.

PA100k vs PETA for Surveillance Use

If forced to choose, PETA is substantially preferable for ITCPR-like data:

  • 647 unique prediction sets vs 7 for PA100k
  • male attribute partially works (15% pos rate) vs gender completely dead in PA100k
  • Age attributes show genuine variation (young/middle-aged spread) vs flat in PA100k
  • Shoe type predictions vary across images (PETA) vs constant in PA100k

Recommended Mitigations

ApproachExpected ImpactEffort
Fine-tune on surveillance data (MARS, DukeMTMC-Attribute)High — resolves distribution shiftHigh
Test-time calibration (adjust per-attribute thresholds based on ITCPR prior)Medium — reduces saturated/dead attrsLow
Temperature scaling on logitsLow — spreads prob mass but doesn't fix featuresLow
Image preprocessing: histogram equalization + sharpening before inferenceLow-Medium — reduces quality gapLow
Replace PromptPAR visual prompts with prompts trained on surveillance dataMedium — keeps architecture, updates priorsMedium

The collapse is fundamentally a domain adaptation problem, not an architecture problem. PromptPAR's design (CLIP + visual/text prompts + MM-former) is sound, but requires the prompts to be adapted to the target domain for reliable predictions.
